The Yangtze River. The longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world, flowing approximately thirty-nine hundred fifteen kilometers across central China from its source in the Tibetan Plateau to the East China Sea. It is the economic and cultural lifeline of China, supporting over one-third of the country's population and serving as a major transportation artery for millennia.

Asia's longest river spans nearly four thousand kilometers from the Tibetan highlands eastward across China to Shanghai. It forms a natural division between northern and southern China, historically shaping distinct regions, cultures, and cuisines. The Yangtze is home to the Three Gorges, a dramatic section of deep canyons that inspired classical Chinese poetry and painting.

The Three Gorges Dam, completed in two thousand six, is the world's largest hydroelectric project, creating a six-hundred-kilometer reservoir. Major cities dot its course—Chongqing, Wuhan, Nanjing, and Shanghai—making it crucial for inland commerce. The Yangtze dolphin, called the baiji and nearly blind, was a freshwater cetacean found only here until it was functionally extinct by the two thousands. The river has been subject to devastating floods that shaped Chinese history, driving the construction and maintenance of dike systems for over two thousand years.
